original_question: Does the luminosity function of gamma-ray bursts evolve with redshift or cosmic time, so that bursts at higher redshift are systematically more luminous than those nearby?
target_in_paper: Does the GRB luminosity function evolve with time?
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the paper’s open question about the evolution of the GRB luminosity function with cosmic time/redshift and captures the notion that bursts at higher redshift may be intrinsically more luminous than those nearby.
missing_details: No specification that the luminosity function refers to the rest-frame isotropic-equivalent peak luminosity distribution φ(L_iso,z)
Lack of definition of the GRB luminosity function (e.g. number density per unit comoving volume per unit luminosity)
Absence of the redshift range over which this question is posed (z≈0.0085–8.2)
No explicit statement of the direction of evolution (i.e. characteristic luminosity increasing with redshift)
Omission of the degeneracy with metallicity bias versus luminosity evolution highlighted in the paper
Missing reference to the context of explaining the observed excess of high-z GRBs relative to the cosmic star formation history
refined_question: Within the observed redshift interval z≈0.0085 to z≈8.2 for long-duration (massive star) gamma-ray bursts, does the rest-frame isotropic-equivalent peak luminosity function φ(L_iso,z) exhibit redshift evolution such that its characteristic luminosity increases systematically with z, after accounting for the standard cosmic star formation history and potential metallicity bias?
justification: Section 2.10 (Cosmological Setting) of the paper explicitly lists “Does the GRB luminosity function evolve with time?” as an open question and notes that one may need to invoke luminosity evolution “so that luminosity is higher at higher-z” to explain the observed excess of high-z GRBs ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1104.0932)). The refined question makes explicit the GRB class (long-duration, massive star GRBs), defines the luminosity function in terms of rest-frame isotropic-equivalent peak luminosity φ(L_iso,z), specifies the relevant redshift range (z≈0.0085–8.2), and clarifies the direction of the evolution implied by the paper.
